title: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez
description: Burke is scheduled to be charged on 31 August. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date.Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen befor
body: Burke is scheduled to be charged on 31 August. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date.Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen before dismembering her body after years of alleged sexual abuse.They allege he killed her because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.Evidence read in court on Monday showed threats Hernandez made to Burke on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl."I swear to GOD I will kill u", one expletive-laden text said, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.During questioning at the hearing on Monday, Detective Corey Farrell of the Los Angeles Police Department said text messages indicated that the defendant and the girl had attended church with her family.  In response to the defence, the detective said he was aware the teen had misrepresented her age to the defendant, telling him she was 16 and 18 at different times.Burke's defence lawyers argued there was not sufficient evidence that he had committed the crime.They said her parents were aware of what was going on between them and had even given written consent for her to travel to London with Burke for a week. The defence highlighted texts on the 22nd and the 23rd of April that suggested Celeste had insisted on going to Burke's Hollywood Hills home and that he had argued against her coming before agreeing to send her an Uber on the night of the 23rd.He "repeatedly expressed love and care for Ms Hernandez after they broke up", defence attorney Marilyn Bednarski said in court.The medical examiner's inability to prove how the two penetrating wounds found in the girl occurred and the lack of surveillance video capturing Burke being home on the night of 23 April showed a lack of evidence, the defence argued.Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that evidence presented during the preliminary hearing provided probable cause for a trial.Burke is charged with murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains."The people have met their burden on all counts," Judge Olmedo said.She found that prosecutors met the threshold for the charge of murder with special circumstances, including lying in wait, motive for financial gain and eliminating a witness.Following the hearing, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office only presented a fraction of the evidence it had against Burke, and that it would present everything in the coming trial.Hochman also said his office had not yet determined if it would pursue the death penalty against Burke.Gruesome images of the girl's dismembered corpse were shown in court during the preliminary hearing.A homicide detective testified that Burke had ordered a body bag, chainsaws, an inflatable pool and a shovel online in the days after Celeste's death.Prosecutors highlighted records that revealed Burke ordered chainsaws and a shovel to his residence after April 23. They allege he used a chainsaw to dismember Hernadez's body.However, Los Angeles Police Department criminalist Lauren Wallace testified that the chainsaws found in his garage tested negative for the presence of blood and were not tested for DNA thereafter, a point the defence highlighted in their attempt to prove the evidence presented was inconclusive.However, investigators were unable to locate a third, 10-inch Makita chainsaw, which prosecutors claim Burke also ordered following Hernandez's death.The BBC's Fame Under Fire podcast brings you the latest from inside the Los Angeles courtroom at the D4vd preliminary hearing.

schema.headline: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez

title: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of h
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of hundreds of prisoners.Burnham announced last week that he was pausing the scheme, which would have seen about 700 prisoners freed in the first phase in September, following a backlash from survivors and victims.But the Conservatives say the government's review will not stop offenders being released. The scheme was part of a bid to stop unprecedented overcrowding, which Labour says was caused by Conservative governments failing to build new prisons.A Labour spokesperson said: "It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess."Early release was first used by the Conservative government, external in 2023 because of prison overcrowding, first for 18 and then 70 days, and 10,000 prisoners had been released early by June 2024 - before Labour came to power.When Sir Keir Starmer entered Downing Street in July 2024, there were fewer than 100 spare prison places across the adult male estate, which is what prompted the Sentencing Act to release another 6,000 prisoners early from September.While the act already excludes the most serious and dangerous offenders, such as murderers serving life sentences or those on extended sentences, the eligibility for early release is based on the length of sentence, external, rather than the type of offence.Badenoch is calling on Burnham to fast-track legislation to keep serious offenders behind bars."It's all well and good cutting bills and bus fares, but that pales into insignificance when paedophiles and rapists are about to be let out on our streets," she is expected to say at a press conference with victims on Tuesday."Burnham needs to show us he's ready to take the tough decisions."Without emergency legislation, Badenoch says dangerous offenders will start to be released the day after MPs return to Parliament after the summer recess on Tuesday 1 September.She is calling on Burnham to revoke legislation coming into effect on 2 September and if necessary recall Parliament to ensure the worst violent and sexual offenders are exempted from early release.Conservative shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "Victims should not have to live in fear all summer waiting for a review."The clock is ticking. Thousands of rapists, paedophiles, and other serious criminals are set to be released in September. "Labour must act now and stop the mass release of dangerous criminals."Earlier this month, the Conservative front bench sought to put pressure on the government to rethink the earlier release plans, saying that it would mean some rapists would leave prison sooner than expected. The government stood by the plan, saying it was a political choice to manage offenders on strict conditions in the community, rather than see the collapse of the system, leaving sex offenders and others to act with impunity.Burnham's decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added.PC Harper's widow Lissie called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.Defending the review of the Sentencing Act that has been announced by Burnham, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives have some nerve. "During their 14 years in office, they shut 23 prisons, created just 482 jail places, and granted early release to 10,000 prisoners - leaving the criminal justice system teetering on verge of collapse."It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess. We have already delivered over 3,000 prison places and we're investing billions to deliver thousands more."Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said: "The reality is that in a properly functioning justice system, no victim or loved ones should ever be told that their perpetrator is being released earlier than expected."Unfortunately, the Conservatives left our prisons on the brink of collapse, creating a capacity crisis that required emergency action to keep the system functioning and the public safe."Now that the government claims to have increased prison capacity, there is a clear opportunity for Burnham to correct some of the mistakes made by his predecessors with this scheme."Reform UK's Home Affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the "disastrous" policy had been introduced by the Tories, and Badenoch had in 2024 supported efforts to expand it."It's clear that only one party has consistently opposed early release and proposed strong law and order reforms to ensure hardened criminals are locked up for the full duration of their sentences," Yusuf said in a statement."Only Reform UK will fix lawless Britain," the party's Home Affairs spokesperson added.

schema.headline: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme

title: Zelensky visit sends clear message of support for Ukraine, Burnham says
description: Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10
body: Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10.Burnham said the visit of the Ukrainian president was designed to "send a very clear message" about the UK's continued support."To put it simply, Volodymyr, I want you to know that we've got your back, you can count on me and you can count on us. You can count on the UK for as long as it takes," he said at a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday.Zelensky, meanwhile, said Ukraine's relationship with the UK was "stronger than ever".Addressing Zelensky, Burnham said: "I am personally with you 100%, Mr President, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."Burnham added that he intended to visit Ukraine "soon" following the "very warm meeting" between the pair.The PM also announced the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.Burnham said: "It will help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives."The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.During Monday's visit, the two leaders also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.Burnham also said the UK would support Ukraine to get a "full and unconditional ceasefire"."We will keep up the pressure, pushing for a ceasefire and a resumption of negotiations which must have Ukraine at the table and include a strong voice for Europe too."Britain's backing of Ukraine has been constant since Russia's invasion four years ago, and the UK has committed £25bn in funding, external for the country's warfighting efforts.In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last Monday, Burnham spoke to Zelensky and invited him to visit the UK "at the earliest opportunity".Zelensky wrote on X shortly afterwards: "I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast."Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader.During that trip, he announced fresh funding worth £255m (€300m) for Ukraine's fight against Russia and was awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom.Asked if he was concerned about changes of leadership in Britain, and in France next year, Zelensky said: "Of course I'm afraid of changes, of course we are afraid because we are in the war each day."But again the priority is the relation between nations, not just between just people. I'm sure that these relations will not change, or we have to do our best not to lose such very good relations."He added: "I hope we will never lose strong relations with the UK during or after the war." Sir Keir replied: "You won't."

schema.headline: Zelensky visit sends clear message of support for Ukraine, Burnham says

title: West Indies v Pakistan: Justin Greaves takes five wickets for none in incredible spell
description: First Test, Tarouba (day three of five)West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 126-7 (Chanderpaul 35, Abbas 3-14)Pakistan 282 (Masood 109; Greaves 5-27)
body: First Test, Tarouba (day three of five)West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 126-7 (Chanderpaul 35, Abbas 3-14)Pakistan 282 (Masood 109; Greaves 5-27)West Indies lead by 155 runsScorecardWest Indies all-rounder Justin Greaves took five wickets without conceding a run in an incredible spell of bowling on day three of the first Test against Pakistan.Greaves, who is playing in his 17th Test, claimed his maiden Test five-wicket haul to help dismiss Pakistan for 282 in response to West Indies' first-innings total of 311.The 32-year-old Barbadian's spell - five consecutive wicket maidens - was all the more remarkable given he had bowled six overs earlier in the day for 27 runs without taking a wicket."When I came on captain Roston Chase just said 'continue to be disciplined in what you are doing' and to see if I can get some wickets for the team," Greaves said."The ball nipped around and I got some reward. Anytime I get the ball in hand the team looks to me to be that solid player for them [and] try to dig us out of situations."To get five wickets for the first time in Test cricket, I'm really happy, but there's still a lot of work to do in the game."Pakistan captain Shan Masood was Greaves' first wicket at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy in Trinidad when he was bowled for 109 in the 64th over following a superb set-up.Greaves had pushed the ball wide to the left-hander from over the wicket before he tailed a delivery back into Masood who played down the wrong line and inside edged on to his stumps.Aamer Jamal had his middle stump uprooted in Greaves' next over as the seamer speared one through his defences.Greaves then trapped Ali Usman lbw before he had Mohammed Rizwan and Mohammad Abbas both caught behind as Pakistan lost their last seven wickets for just 38 runs.West Indies reached stumps on day three on 126-7 in their second innings - a lead of 155 runs - to leave the match finely poised.

schema.headline: West Indies v Pakistan: Justin Greaves takes five wickets for none in incredible spell

title: John Stones: England defender in advanced talks to join Inter Milan
description: England defender John Stones is in advanced talks with Inter Milan about joining the Italian side on a free transfer.The centre-half is a free agent a
body: England defender John Stones is in advanced talks with Inter Milan about joining the Italian side on a free transfer.The centre-half is a free agent after leaving Manchester City at the end of June.Stones has been the subject of major interest from clubs across Europe, including Chelsea and Juventus.But Serie A champions Inter have held positive discussions with the 32-year-old and are understood to be leading the race to sign the Premier League and Champions League winner on a two-year contract. Stones made 295 appearances for City after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016.He helped City win six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, five League Cups, three Community Shields, the Club World Cup and the Uefa Super Cup.The former Barnsley defender has won 93 international caps and was part of the England squad who finished third at the World Cup.

schema.headline: John Stones: England defender in advanced talks to join Inter Milan

title: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress
description: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with t
body: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with the sun disappearing behind", with an "orange-like filter" over the city.Though De Abreu said he is less concerned about his flat which lies on the other side of the river, he "can see a number of people worried about what is to come".Elsewhere, Rachel Hanberry told BBC Radio 5 Live that her beachfront home in Biscarrosse Plage, which lies about 63km (40 miles) from Bordeaux, is located next to the town's evacuation point. "Everyone came here on Thursday night," she said. "People had nowhere to go. We offered our home to people."The community there has "lost so much", she added. "The stress and trauma that you feel as someone living here is immense." About 700km away, in Cotignac in the south-east of France, Jo Barnes and her family returned to their home on Saturday, having evacuated for four days after a fire rapidly moved towards their property. "A wall of orange flames came roaring up over the hill," Barnes said. "On Friday afternoon, the fire came back to our area... within 10 metres of the back of our house, we have a gas tank here, it was all very dramatic." Though the surrounding hillside was blackened and charred, the town of Cotignac was undamaged and the Barnes' family home left intact. In the central Madrid region of Spain, where more than 27,000 hectares (66,000 acres) have burnt, residents have faced similar ordeals. "Everyone had to get out of the village quickly, it was a critical situation and people were scared," Olga Congacha told AFP news agency.She and her husband did not take much: "[We] left with all that we could grab, our important documents, some clothes".In the eastern Castellón province, Ricardo Pozo told AFP that he had "never seen a fire this intense before". "I've seen major fires, but on television. Nothing like this, here and now." Maria Garcia, who lives in Betxí - also in the Castellón province - described to Reuters how the fires had put life on pause for those who evacuated: "You can't go out to work, you can't go about your daily life." "You can see the mountains you've known your whole life burning," she added.The wildfires have also upended plans for holidaymakers. James Hillier had been visiting his son in the seaside community of Lacanau about 42 km (26 miles) east of Bordeaux in the Gironde department."The whole town got consumed by smoke," he told the BBC. "There was ash falling from the sky and I noticed a big lump of it landed on my hand."He and his wife left the town for Bordeaux on Saturday, but found that in the city "the air was acrid - it stung your eyes and people were wearing masks". They have since left to go to somewhere in the north of the France instead. Sarah from Hertfordshire realised that her family would have to cut their week-long holiday in Bordeaux short because of the smoke. "We sealed all the apartment up, but it still had a really strong smell of smoke everywhere. It was quite worrying," she said.She then warned her sister-in-law Georgia, whose family had been due to join them in the Bordeaux region in Lacanau, not to come. Georgia booked to stay in another region instead.Georgia said she has not been able to secure a refund from her accommodation operator because the fire had not yet reached Lacanau at the time of cancellation. "If we don't find a solution with them we currently stand to lose over £3,500," Georgia added.

schema.headline: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress

title: Jack Draper: Long-term arm injury rules former British number one out of Mubadala DC Open
description: The former world number four has only played 14 matches in the past 12 months, largely because of the bruised humerus which he has tried to overcome b
body: The former world number four has only played 14 matches in the past 12 months, largely because of the bruised humerus which he has tried to overcome by resting for long periods."It's hard to tell when you can push [and] when not to push," Draper said at Wimbledon."At the end of the day I'm playing a very aggressive sport, that you need to play through some stuff. Sometimes it's too much. Sometimes it's not."I wouldn't be competing anywhere if there was a chance that I'm going to get a lot worse, for instance."Draper's initial comeback earlier this season was derailed by tendinitis in his knee and the three-time ATP Tour winner had not played for more than two months before his return at Eastbourne in June.Reaching the semi-finals came at a price, though, with his arm injury flaring up again at Wimbledon and leaving Draper "devastated" at having to pull out of his home Grand Slam.Draper, who is now ranked 147th in the world, has not played a major since the US Open in August.If he is fit enough to play at Flushing Meadows this year, he will have to come through qualifying - or be given a wildcard - to play in the main draw.In Washington, Draper will be replaced in the draw by lucky loser Mackenzie McDonald.

schema.headline: Jack Draper: Long-term arm injury rules former British number one out of Mubadala DC Open

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty says 'nothing makes sense' after another bronze
description: Ramsay-Peaty is the greatest breaststroker of all time, having gone eight years unbeaten in the 100m and holding the world record in that event and th
body: Ramsay-Peaty is the greatest breaststroker of all time, having gone eight years unbeaten in the 100m and holding the world record in that event and the 50m.He was the defending Commonwealth champion in the 50m and decided to continue in the sport because it was added to the 2028 Olympic schedule.On Saturday he suggested the shorter distance would provide his best chance of a medal in Los Angeles, given his age."I thought I could have done better there," Ramsay-Peaty said after finishing in 26.94 seconds - 0.44secs behind Williamson."It is quite disappointing in terms of the time, and, as we know, times equal medals."I felt I could have been a little quicker, but I need to look at it and see what is going on because nothing makes sense this week to be honest."Ramsay-Peaty dominated the events under the coaching of Mel Marshall, who relocated to Australia in 2024.After the Paris 2024 Olympics, Ramsay-Peaty began training at Repton in Derbyshire but has since moved back to London to the tutelage of Lisa Bates."I am very, very happy, couldn't be happier with where I am training now," said Ramsay-Peaty."It is hard work, but we need to make sure that hard work is going in the right place."These things don't happen in three months; they happen in two years and we need to make sure we keep investing."Meanwhile, there was gold for England's Brock Whiston in the women's 200m breaststroke SB8 final, with 15-year-old team-mate Iona Winnifrith taking bronze.Amalie Smith, 16, took silver in the women's 200m individual medley final, and the England quartet of Freya Colbert, Abbie Wood, Leah Schlosshan and Freya Anderson won silver in the women's 4x200m freestyle relay.

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty says 'nothing makes sense' after another bronze

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Race against time' and 'We've lost a Goodie'
description: The Times, external features an article by Prime Minister Andy Burnham about his plans to promote more vocational education for teenagers from the age
body: The Times, external features an article by Prime Minister Andy Burnham about his plans to promote more vocational education for teenagers from the age of 14. In it, the prime minister says the country will "value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap". He goes on to say that getting the plans right will make the difference between people believing they can realise their talents or "growing up believing there was never a place for them to begin with"."Burnham axes Blair's university vision" is the Daily Telegraph's, external front page headline on the story, while the Guardian, external says the prime minister will tell schools to adapt their curriculum to the needs of local businesses. The Financial Times, external notes that previous governments, both Conservative and Labour, were unconvinced by the policy when Burnham introduced similar plans in Greater Manchester.The Sun's, external editorial says Burnham's vow to make benefit claimants face tougher hurdles has become pressing. It says the prime minister's biggest challenge "will be forcing even these modest proposals past his delusional backbench MPs". The Daily Mail, external includes an article by Reform UK's treasury spokesman, Robert Jenrick, who warns Burnham against introducing a 10% estate tax, for which he has previously expressed support, to pay for social care. Jenrick calls it "every pensioner's worst nightmare".A dramatic image of the wildfires in France features on the front page of the i Paper, external, beneath the headline "Race against Time". The Guardian's, external report says fleeing the wildfires "felt like a disaster movie".Many papers pay tribute to Bill Oddie. The i Paper, external remembers the former Springwatch presenter as "the man who made Britain fall back in love with birds". His earlier career as a member of the comedy troupe the Goodies is frequently referenced. The front page of the Daily Star, external says "we've lost a goodie", and for the Mirror, external it's "a goodie innings". The Daily Express, external editorial says "it's quite an achievement to be admired and respected in one career, but to do it again in another is remarkable".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Race against time' and 'We've lost a Goodie'

title: Attachment theory explained and how to become secure
description: Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help youImage source, Lizzy SmithImage caption, Lizzy Smith says she used to see her diff
body: Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help youImage source, Lizzy SmithImage caption, Lizzy Smith says she used to see her difficulty with relationships as "completely unsolvable"ByJosh ElginFor Lizzy, relationships always seemed to end the same way. "I would get to a second or third date and find something wrong with them." Just as things began to feel real, the connection she longed for would suddenly feel uncomfortable, even threatening. And she would pull away.For years, she couldn't explain why - until she came across attachment theory.And it was the description of a so-called fearful-avoidant - one of the four attachment styles - which felt strikingly familiar.It describes someone who wants closeness, but worries that people in their life will eventually reject or abandon them."It was like I had found the missing piece to a puzzle that I've been trying to solve for years," Lizzy says.She is not alone. Attachment theory has exploded into the public consciousness.On TikTok, videos tagged #AttachmentTheory have racked up hundreds of millions of views.And in popular culture it's used to explain everything from Marianne and Connell's relationship in the hit book and TV series Normal People to the lyrics of Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's record-breaking number one track Rein Me In."The first time I listened to it I started crying," Lizzy says.For her, the song gave voice to both sides of avoidant attachment: the fear that can make love feel unbearable, and the confusion felt by the partner left behind.What are the four attachment styles?First developed in the 1950s by British psychiatrist John Bowlby, attachment theory suggests that the bonds we form with early caregivers shape our expectations of relationships.If support is consistently available, you are more likely to see others as reliable. If care is unpredictable or emotionally distant, you may develop strategies designed to protect yourself from disappointment or distress.There are four attachment styles - anxious, avoidant, fearful-avoidant and secure. In simple terms they are defined as follows:Anxious attachment is often associated with worries about rejection or abandonment. People with this attachment style may seek frequent reassurance from those close to them and struggle with low self-worth. They can be highly attuned to changes in other people's behaviour.People with an avoidant attachment style prioritise their independence and find it difficult to open up emotionally or rely on others. They may subconsciously view intimacy as a threat to their autonomy and withdraw when relationships become too emotionally close.Those with fearful-avoidant attachment (also known as disorganised) want close relationships but often struggle to feel safe in them. They may seek connection one moment and withdraw the next. Someone who is secure is comfortable with both closeness and independence in relationships. They are generally able to trust others, communicate their needs and seek support when they need it.Research suggests that secure people tend to fare better not only in romantic relationships, but across life. They manage stress more effectively, cope better with setbacks like rejection or loss and are better colleagues and managers in the workplace.And what began as a way to understand relationships is increasingly influencing how people navigate them.Across social media, attachment styles are used to reassess friendships, make sense of family tensions or rule out potential partners.And relationship coaches promise to reveal the hidden signs of emotional unavailability in a partner or the ways to heal anxious attachment.The misconceptions around attachment theoryDr Pascal Vrticka, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Essex, has spent nearly two decades studying attachment.He says the theory offers "one of the best explanations" for the differences in how people seek support and connection with others.And while he's glad to see it reach a wider audience, he worries the way it is interpreted can be "outdated, misinformed and, in the worst case, harmful.""I think one problem is that people are overgeneralising it and using it in contexts where it might not be the best framework to explain our behaviour," he says.Part of the issue, he explains, is that initial assumptions around attachment theory have evolved since it was first developed.Vrticka says one of the biggest misconceptions is that attachment styles are fixed.Although studies have found that they can show a degree of stability over time, Vrticka says change is possible."The good news is that the evidence shows that secure attachment is the most stable. Which means that once you become secure, you tend to stay secure."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sam Fender and Olivia Dean accept the BRIT Award for song of the year for Rein Me In, which has been dubbed an "avoidant anthem."He says attachment is often reshaped during periods of transition, particularly during adolescence, when young people begin forming close relationships beyond their family.Later events in our lives, like entering a new relationship, experiencing a breakup or dealing with bereavement, can also be influential.But Vrticka says that change is gradual and professional support is likely to be needed for people with more entrenched attachment patterns.It's that nuance, Lizzy says, which is often lost in discussions of attachment theory.She says some people can be "quick to assume the worst" and reduce others to labels. However, while she says people with insecure attachment styles should be viewed with more empathy, she acknowledges the importance of self-awareness. "For me, I know that my avoidant tendencies are toxic and it would be unfair for me to date someone right now," she says.But, she adds, that doesn't mean people with insecure attachments are incapable of healthy relationships. "It is on you to acknowledge it and put in the work to heal."How do you become secure?Few have played a more influential role in bringing attachment to the mainstream than Dr Amir Levine.His book Attached, co-written with Rachel Heller, was first published in 2010 and has since sold millions of copies around the world.But in his latest book, Levine shifts the focus from identifying attachment styles to ask a different question: how do you become secure?Part of the answer, he argues, lies in what he calls "SIMIs" - seemingly insignificant minor interactions.A text from a friend asking about your weekend. A smile from a stranger."The brain monitors small interactions all the time," Levine says. "That's what attachment is about. It's a monitoring system for safety."And he says these interactions gradually shape what the brain expects from relationships.Positive experiences build evidence that people can be trusted and relied upon, helping move someone towards what he calls "secure mode".Image source, Shira H. WeissImage caption, After helping millions identify their attachment style, Amir Levine is now focused on how those patterns can changeBut equally, a delayed response or a friend failing to follow through on plans can trigger subtle stress responses in the nervous system.Importantly, Levine says it's possible to have different attachment styles with different people.So he encourages people to identify the relationships in their lives that already make them feel safe and understood, and to use them "as a vehicle for becoming more secure overall".And the idea that security can be built through current relationships reflects a broader shift away from seeing attachment as just the result of childhood experiences.For some, discovering attachment theory can involve re-examining family relationships, which can potentially lead to resentment. But Levine says "it's not just about where you started, but what happens afterwards"."If that way of thinking helps you understand yourself and move forward, that's useful," he says."But if it makes you feel stuck or damaged, then it's not accurate because people really can change."Levine also argues that insecure attachments can in themselves be strengths.Complex with Kimberley WilsonWhat is anxious attachment?He says anxious people are often acutely tuned into relationships, spotting subtle shifts in mood, tone and behaviour that others miss, while avoidant people can be fiercely independent and perform well under pressure.However, whilst Vrticka agrees that attachment styles shouldn't be seen as either good or bad, he stresses they "come with certain risks and difficulties", which he says shouldn't be disregarded.But both agree that attachment theory is most useful when it helps people understand patterns rather than define themselves.

schema.headline: Attachment theory explained and how to become secure

title: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeout
description: English football will implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season.The Football Association, Premier League, Engl
body: English football will implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season.The Football Association, Premier League, English Football League, National League and Women's Super League have agreed on the measure, with permission granted by the International Football Association Board (Ifab).Pro Ref, led by chief refereeing officer Howard Webb, had been in discussions with the leagues to determine how to tackle the issue. It settled on a team having to remove an outfield player from the pitch. If a referee signals that the physio can come on to treat a goalkeeper, that team's coach will have 10 seconds to nominate another player to leave the pitch for one minute after play has restarted, telling the fourth official of their choice.If no player has been selected within 10 seconds, the captain must leave the field.The first game to feature the trial will be the Carabao Cup preliminary round tie between Tranmere and Rochdale on Saturday.BBC Sport understands that the Australian A-League will trial a variation with the captain always having to leave the field.The tactic of gaining a timeout as the keeper is treated has become increasingly common and controversial in recent seasons.It has not been uncommon for the goalkeeper to sit on the turf and signal for the physio, with all the other players rushing to the technical area for a team talk. As soon as the coach has delivered their instructions, the keeper gets up to play on.Goalkeeper treatment has also been used to disrupt the opposition's momentum when they are on top.In November, Leeds United boss Daniel Farke accused Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma of feigning injury to "bend the rules" and break up play.Ifab, meanwhile, has issued a clarification to the mistaken identity rule after Fifa used it to book two players for simulation at the World Cup.Paraguay's Miguel Almiron and Breel Embolo of Switzerland both received bookings. Embolo was already on a caution meaning he was sent off in the quarter-final defeat by Argentina.Ifab says that while it was well received and will be included in the detailed review of the VAR protocol, it "may not be used as such until that review is concluded".At Ifab's AGM in February, head of referees Pierluigi Collina said finding a solution to stop the goalkeeper tactical timeout was a priority.At the 2026 World Cup, Collina told his officials to prevent players from going to the technical area on all stoppages.The effectiveness of the measure is open to debate, as the three-minute hydration breaks in each half created a natural opportunity for a team talk.In its own discussions, English football felt that merely stopping players going to the technical area would not deter coaches from using goalkeepers to break up play.English football chose this trial as it follows the logic applied to outfield players, who must themselves leave the field for one minute if the physio comes on.It is intended to be proactive as a deterrent rather than reactive to a team talk as it happens. Match of the Day pundit Danny Murphy suggested last season that lawmakers could act to close the loophole in this exact way."I think they can change it really quickly," Murphy said. "If a keeper goes down injured, instead of him having to go off, one of the outfield players should go off then it's fair all round. "It's a little change that makes a world of difference."Officials will not prevent players from visiting the touchline as an injury is treated but it is hoped the prospect of playing with 10 players for a minute will act as an adequate disincentive.This is especially the case in the final minutes of games, when teams trying to hold on to a result would use the goalkeeper to kill momentum. Now they would have to play with 10 players.There are a few exemptions when a team-mate will not have to go off.Where a goalkeeper says they do not need the physio and they have not caused play to stopThe goalkeeper and an outfield player have collidedIf a goalkeeper is fouled and needs immediate treatmentIf a goalkeeper is bleedingIf there is a serious injury (has to be substituted) or concussion.If the goalkeeper is substituted, the substitution is not delayed.There have been some concerns that a requirement to leave the field for one minute could lead to players, both goalkeepers and outfield, attempting to play on with an injury. The results of the trials will be assessed by Ifab at its meetings throughout the seasons, and this could lead to a permanent law change globally from 2027-28.

schema.headline: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeout

title: Liverpool: Centre-back situation and why Andoni Iraola must act to bring in experience
description: Two centre-backs caught the eye of Liverpool's scouting department at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last November.Within weeks, the club spent a combined
body: Two centre-backs caught the eye of Liverpool's scouting department at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last November.Within weeks, the club spent a combined £3.5m on the pair: Senegal's Mor Talla Ndiaye and Austria's Ifeanyi Ndukwe.Under Matt Newberry, Liverpool's director of global talent, this was evidence of future planning in full flow.Yet surely no-one inside the club would have expected the teenage duo to be the centre-back pairing for most of Liverpool's opening pre-season fixture.With Joe Gomez forced off by injury in the eighth minute against Sunderland, and neither Jeremy Jacquet or Giovanni Leoni fit to play still, Liverpool have a problem at the heart of their defence.Looking at the long term is one thing, but they need reinforcements in the here and now.Even before the injury, new head coach Andoni Iraola said his squad was "very thin" defensively.Gomez was absent from Liverpool's training session in Chicago on Sunday and an update on the severity of his injury is expected this week.He is Liverpool's longest-serving current player but has now missed 225 games because of injury, according to Transfermarkt, since signing from Charlton in 2015.Virgil van Dijk is the club's only fit senior centre-back. The Liverpool captain is 35 and played every minute in the Premier League last season, but he is not the force that he used to be.The Dutchman, like Gomez, is also into the last year of his contract at Anfield. There is a possibility both players will move on next summer.One of the reasons why Liverpool allowed Ibrahima Konate to leave on a free transfer and join Real Madrid was because they felt Jacquet, 21, and Leoni, 19, whose transfers weighed in at £60m and £26m respectively, were the best young centre-backs in France and Italy.Perhaps they will prove inspired signings, with Jacquet in line to make his debut against Leeds on Sunday.Liverpool will give them every opportunity to fulfil their potential, but right now, just like Ndiaye and Ndukwe, both are far from the finished product."We need players. It's fairly obvious," former Liverpool striker Robbie Fowler told BBC Sport in New York, where the Reds take on Wrexham on Wednesday."I'm very sad for Joe Gomez, who has been so unfortunate with injuries. This could have been a real chance to cement his place and for him to show that we don't need another centre-half."We've spent money on Jacquet and Leoni and the guidance that Joe and Virgil can give from their experience to the young lads is telling."We won't see the best version of the young lads yet, but you do need that experience in the squad. And yes, the manager's been on record saying that we need players and I would not be surprised if another centre-half is in that conversation."From the outside, Liverpool's failure to seal a move for Marc Guehi last summer looks even more interesting now.They have a buyback clause with Jarell Quansah, who left for Bayer Leverkusen for £35m last July, but there are no current plans for Quansah to return.Sources stress that if Liverpool bring in Bradley Barcola, who Paris St-Germain value in excess of £100m, then there will be limitations to what more they can do in the market.Deals for Jacquet and Victor Munoz have cost a combined £94.5m.Without any major outgoings from Iraola's squad, there is an understanding that this summer will not be like last summer when a club record £450m was spent.Fowler, who scored 183 times for the Reds, said: "When you look at Liverpool across the last decade, one of the problems that we've had is that the first 11 is more than capable but the argument that people have is the squad depth."I'm a big believer in getting the squad right because it gives everyone a lift and keeps people on their toes, knowing that if you're not performing, someone else could do the job."Go back to the days of Phil Neal and he'll tell you stories about how players would never want to get injured because they knew that if someone else came, they wouldn't get their place back."You need that mentality and I think that has a real knock-on effect on standards."In six months from last summer through to January 2026, Liverpool agreed deals for five centre-backs who were aged 20 or under at the time - Leoni, Ndiaye, Ndukwe, Noah Adekoya and Jacquet.It is worth noting that Ndukwe, who was impressive against Sunderland, must go out on loan this year as he does not yet meet the criteria for a UK work permit.The long-term potential of centre-backs is not a concern at Anfield.But experience is in short supply - a glaring gap in this Liverpool squad and one that needs to be addressed.

schema.headline: Liverpool: Centre-back situation and why Andoni Iraola must act to bring in experience

title: Chelsea transfer news: Henderson, Welbeck, Lacroix - why do Blues want older players now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chelsea look set to complete a free transfer for Brentford midfielder Jordan Henderson (left), with Brighton'
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chelsea look set to complete a free transfer for Brentford midfielder Jordan Henderson (left), with Brighton's Danny Welbeck also emerging as a transfer targetBySimon CassonBBC Sport senior journalistChelsea are targeting deals for Maxence Lacroix, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson - and the ages of the experienced trio seem to signal a major change in transfer tactics from the Blues.At 26, it could be said that Crystal Palace and France defence Lacroix is in his prime, but the £52m target is still notably older than other recent Blues signings.It has been two years since Chelsea signed a player older than Lacroix, and Tosin Adarabioyo was only marginally older when he arrived three months before turning 27.Meanwhile, Brighton striker Welbeck is 35 and keen to move to Stamford Bridge, and Brentford and England midfielder Henderson is 36.Welbeck's potential arrival could mean he replaces 23-year-old Liam Delap in the first-team picture.That is despite Delap having been considered one of the Premier League's most exciting young strikers when Chelsea signed him from Ipswich Town last year.So does this signal a deliberate change in recruitment strategy - prioritising experience over youth? And what might Chelsea have learned from recent seasons.The summer of 2022 - Tuchel goes for experienceImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chelsea spent over £90m in signing Raheem Sterling, Kalidou Koulibaly and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang in the summer of 2022In the months that followed the club's takeover four years ago, then manager Thomas Tuchel went on a spending spree.His first major signing was Manchester City winger Raheem Sterling - aged 27 at the time - for up to £50m including add-ons. After winning four Premier League titles at City and helping England reach the semi-finals of the 2018 World Cup, there was much excitement.Sterling at Chelsea didn't work out though. Despite moments of brilliance, Sterling struggled for form and fitness as the team went on to finish 12th in the 2022-23 season.For a player reportedly earning over £300,000 a week, his performances fell well short of expectations. Sterling eventually left on a free transfer in January 2026.Kalidou Koulibaly's arrival from Napoli for £33m also didn't end well. Rated at the time as one of European club football's top centre-backs, the Senegalese player - then 31 - was out of the door after just one season, joining Al-Hilal.Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang is another experienced player whose time at Stamford Bridge was short-lived. The former AC Milan, Borussia Dortmund and Arsenal striker signed from Barcelona for £10.3m on the final day of the summer transfer window - just days before Tuchel's sacking.Aubameyang - 33 when he joined - struggled to find form or game time under subsequent bosses Graham Potter and Frank Lampard and, like Sterling, ended up leaving the club on a free transfer.Post 2022 - a focus on youth Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chelsea switched their focus to signing younger players in 2022 with Enzo Fernandez, Moises Caicedo and Cole Palmer joining the clubAfter such a poor return from their investment, it is perhaps no surprise that there was a shift in recruitment policy, as Chelsea switched their focus to signing younger players.Let's start here with the success stories.Chelsea made a major investment in a World Cup winner in January 2023 when they signed Argentina star Enzo Fernandez from Benfica for a then-British record fee of £107m. The move came just two weeks after his 22nd birthday.Across the 2024-25 and 2025-26 seasons, Fernandez registered an impressive 24 assists in all competitions - including the Club World Cup - trailing only Bruno Fernandes and Mohamed Salah among Premier League players.Chelsea made another nine-figure move just seven months later to sign Moises Caicedo - then 21 - from Brighton.His £100m price tag - rising to a potential £115m - seemed hard to justify at first as the Ecuadorian had a slow start at Stamford Bridge.Since then, Caicedo has established himself as one of the Premier League's leading midfielders.Caicedo was the joint leader for interceptions in the Premier League last season (59, the same number as James Garner of Everton).The initial £40m the club paid Manchester City for Cole Palmer - also 21 at the time in September 2023 - has also looked like money well spent.Palmer was the club's top scorer in his first season.Only Erling Haaland (76), Salah (54) and Ollie Watkins (51) have scored more goals than Palmer, with 47, in the Premier League since he joined.Then there are the signings that haven't worked out.Mykhailo Mudryk was 22 when he joined Chelsea from Shakhtar Donetsk for an initial fee of £62m, potentially rising to £89m including add-ons. The Ukraine winger, now 25, has been sidelined for over 18 months after an "adverse finding in a routine urine test" led to a provisional suspension in December 2024.The winger has since been served with a four-year ban by the Football Association and has lodged an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport.Joao Felix struggled to make an impact during two stints at Chelsea. His first loan spell in 2023 at the age of 23 started with a red card in his first game.A permanent move followed a year later but he struggled to justify the fee - somewhere in the region of £45m - and scored just once in 12 Premier League games before being sold to Al-Nassr.After joining from Leicester for about £70m at the age of 21, Wesley Fofana's time at Chelsea has been plagued by injury.The France international, who was not selected for his country's World Cup squad, could be under scrutiny as the club look to reduce the size of their squad.The past four seasons - a pattern of inconsistencyFor a club to have spent as much as Chelsea, it is no surprise fans might be frustrated with the returns - or lack of them.The 12th-placed Premier League finish in 2022-23 - the first season since the takeover by the BlueCo consortium - was clearly a big disappointment.Improvements followed, with sixth and fourth in the next two campaigns signalling strides in the right direction, but finishing 10th last season was another big blow.Since 2022, Chelsea have won two trophies: the Conference League and the Club World Cup.But for owners with such big ambitions, they will surely feel like their expectations haven't yet been met.The Alonso era - back to ready-to-go signings?If his previous managerial approach is anything to go by, Xabi Alonso favours a blend of youth and experience.The Spaniard signed four players over the age of 27 for the 2023-24 season at Bayer Leverkusen. They included Granit Xhaka and Alejandro Grimaldo - two key players in their Bundesliga title-winning side.Another four players over the age of 27 came the following season.It could be a similar story now at Chelsea.Alonso shaping squad as he wants it - analysisByFootball reporterOwner Behdad Eghbali said Chelsea would "tweak" their model and add experience to what he still believes is a strong core of young players, including Cole Palmer, Moises Caicedo and Levi Colwill.Welbeck joining Chelsea would be another sign of a shift in strategy.Their move for him follows attempts to sign 33-year-old midfielder Granit Xhaka from Sunderland, with the Black Cats refusing to sell the Switzerland captain.Although the arrival of Rogers, 23, fits the club's preferred policy of signing younger players, he brings significant Premier League experience.The Blues are also expected to complete a £52m move for Lacroix, 26 - further Premier League-ready experience.It is clear that Welbeck's arrival would leave Chelsea with an abundance of attacking options for a season when they are not involved in European competition so do not necessarily need such resources.At his age, Welbeck may be content to provide cover for Joao Pedro, but the move would represent bad news for several other forwards.Nicolas Jackson is open to leaving, while Delap and Emmanuel Emegha had hoped to establish themselves under Alonso.Nevertheless, the Chelsea manager is getting what he wants: experience and strong personalities to address shortcomings that contributed to the team's 10th-place finish in the Premier League last season.Additional reporting by Matt Jones

schema.headline: Chelsea transfer news: Henderson, Welbeck, Lacroix - why do Blues want older players now?

title: Wu Chi-wai: Hong Kong activist allowed to stay in UK after deportation threat
description: Former Hong Kong opposition leader Wu Chi-wai has been allowed to stay in the UK with his family for six months, after initially being detained at the
body: Former Hong Kong opposition leader Wu Chi-wai has been allowed to stay in the UK with his family for six months, after initially being detained at the border.Wu had arrived at London's Heathrow Airport last Wednesday, where he was detained for nearly 10 hours and initially refused entry, he told BBC Chinese. He said he was later told he could stay for only one week, after which he would have to report to the airport to be deported.But on Monday, the UK Border Force approved his entry and granted him a standard stay of six months, he said.The 63-year-old was the leader of the now-defunct Democratic Party and one of the most recognisable faces of the city's quashed pro-democracy movement.Wu is one of the so-called Hong Kong 47, a group of high-profile pro-democracy leaders who were sentenced to jail after a controversial national security trial.He was released in June after spending more than five years in prison for subversion and other convictions.Wu told BBC Chinese that his son and wife moved to the UK in 2022 and 2023, and the only communication he had with them since then was through monthly phone calls and letters. He had hoped to reunite with his family in the UK during his recent visit, he added.Ahead of his departure, Wu said he had consulted staff at the British Consulate General in Hong Kong, asking if there would be any problems with his entry."The information I received was that there would be none," he said, adding that consular staff said they would explain his criminal record and itinerary to the UK Border Force.The Border Force said he was not considered a "genuine visitor" who was solely visiting family, he said.Wu denies that he had intended to apply for political asylum in the UK - a claim that was previously reported in the media.Rights group Hong Kong Watch, which had called on UK authorities to allow Wu to stay in the country, said in a statement that it welcomed the recent news."This is the right outcome, and it should never have taken this long," Megan Khoo, Hong Kong Watch's policy director, said in a statement on Monday. "He should never have faced the prospect of removal back to the city that jailed him."Wu was using his British National (Overseas) (BNO) passport - a special travel document issued to Hong Kong permanent residents before 1 July 1997, when Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule - to enter the UK. BNO passport holders are typically allowed to stay in the UK visa-free for six months.Since 2021, the UK government launched a visa programme for BNO passport holders. Those granted the visa are eligible to work, study and live in the UK, putting them on a pathway to citizenship after they settle in the UK.The new policy came after Hong Kong was rocked by massive pro-democracy protests, which authorities cracked down on. Since then, Hong Kong has come under increasing control from Beijing, and many of its pro-democracy figures have been either fled the city or been jailed.More than 230,000 Hong Kongers have been granted BNO visas and nearly 170,000 have already relocated to the UK, according to the UK government. The UK Home Office, which oversees the UK Border Force, told BBC Chinese on Monday that it does not comment on individual cases, but stated that "the UK government remains steadfast in its support for the Hong Kong community in the UK".A spokesperson from HKSAR Government told BBC Chinese that it has not received any requests for assistance from Hong Kong residents to date.

schema.headline: Wu Chi-wai: Hong Kong activist allowed to stay in UK after deportation threat
